title: Stratus Bank — Dedicated Capacity Discovery
summary: Discovery call to evaluate Redwood Dedicated for model serving at Stratus Bank. Discussed reserved GPU requirements, isolation and data residency, burst strategy and autoscaling, expected qps/latency, security controls (SOC2/KMS/SSO), cost tradeoffs vs hosted, and next steps for benchmarks and pricing.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I run sales for the east coast accounts, and with me is Ravi from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Elena (Stratus): Hi Maya, thanks. I'm Elena, head of ML at Stratus Bank. We have Tom and Priya on as well.
[00:10] Tom (Stratus): Hey.
[00:12] Priya (Stratus): Hi, thanks for making time.
[00:14] Maya: Quick agenda — want to understand your current stack, what workloads you want to run, whether you need isolation or private deployment, sizing for reserved GPUs, burst strategy, and then talk next steps. Sound good?
[00:22] Elena: Yep, good. We're looking to move from a pilot on hosted endpoints to a dedicated capacity model for production. Mainly transformer-based models for document understanding, redaction, and some chat assistants for internal ops.
[00:30] Maya: Great. Can you tell us current scale? QPS, concurrency, and any latency targets?
[00:35] Elena: Our baseline is small today — maybe 5 to 10 rps for internal apps, but we expect to ramp to 200 rps within 6 months for batch/async workloads and peaks up to ~500 rps during end-of-month processing. Latency target for interactive tools is sub-300ms per request 95th, for batch it's okay to be higher.
[00:52] Ravi (Redwood SE): Okay that's helpful. For 200–500 rps, we usually look at dedicated pools with autoscale and burst policies. A couple clarifying Qs: are you doing long context windows? KV cache heavy workflows? And what's your average prompt+response token size?
[01:05] Elena: Context windows up to 8k tokens sometimes; most calls are around 1k tokens. We do a fair amount of KV caching across sessions for chat history, and some retrieval-augmented generation where we attach doc chunks.
[01:17] Tom: Also, data residency is important — models can't send raw customer PII outside our VPC. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). What's the difference operationally?
[01:27] Maya: Short answer — Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity in Redwood's environment but logically isolated per tenant with data separation and encryption; Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and can run inside your VPC or on-prem. Dedicated is faster to onboard and supports reserved SLAs, Private is for strict residency/air-gapped needs.
[01:42] Priya: For compliance we need KMS integration and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Do you support customer-managed KMS and exportable audit logs?
[01:50] Ravi: Yes — for Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping and we provide audit logs, and we can ship logs to your S3 or SIEM. For Private deployments you have full control. There are some details re: egress path and support model, we'll share the security pack.
[02:05] Elena: Cost is a big concern. We saw hosted pricing from Redwood but wanted to understand committed costs for Dedicated and what burst looks like. Can you explain reserved GPU tiers and burst/overflow mechanisms?
[02:16] Maya: Sure. Dedicated is monthly reserved capacity — e.g., 4x A100-equivalent nodes gives you steady throughput and predictable per-token unit costs. We offer burst credits and a burst pool so you can exceed reserved for short windows at a premium. There's also automatic fallback to hosted model variants if you hit capacity and have that policy enabled.
[02:32] Ravi: In practice, we size pools by expected steady-state throughput and add a headroom buffer. For end-of-month peaks customers either configure a burst pool or we recommend short-term capacity add-ons. We can also use model quantization and batching to lower per-token cost and increase throughput.
[02:45] Tom: For our workloads, the 8k contexts will increase memory per model instance. Do you select kernels and quantization per model/runtime? Any multi-tenancy interference concerns?
[02:54] Ravi: The runtime picks optimized kernels and we support per-tenant quantization profiles. Dedicated pools isolate GPU hosts so you shouldn't see noisy neighbor interference. For VMs we pin to GPUs and manage KV cache per model instance. There are operational knobs around sequence length and batch sizing that matter.
[03:10] Elena: What's the typical time to scale up capacity? If we want to add 100% capacity for a short window, how fast can that happen?
[03:16] Maya: For Dedicated, scaling plan depends on commit and available capacity in region. Autoscaling within your pool is usually seconds to minutes for allocating queued requests across nodes, but provisioning new reserved nodes takes longer — days — unless you have burst credits or short-term on-demand capacity.
[03:30] Priya: For audits, we need SOC2 compliance evidence and data flow diagrams. Also SSO and RBAC integration. We will need contractual terms about where logs and model outputs are stored.
[03:40] Ravi: We have SOC2 Type II reports and ISO references we can share. Redwood supports SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC with token-level auditing. We'll include a network diagram and dataflow references in the security pack.
[03:52] Tom: Can you touch on fallback policies? If the Dedicated pool is full do requests fail or route to hosted? We can't afford a hard failure for internal ops.
[04:00] Maya: We recommend automatic fallback to a hosted-compatible model variant with configured latency/cost tradeoffs. For critical paths you can also implement graceful degradation — shorter contexts, smaller model variant, or rate-limit noncritical requests. We can set up route policies per endpoint.
[04:12] Elena: For quality, how do you handle canary rollouts and evals so we don't regress? We need to tie regressions to specific prompt sets.
[04:20] Ravi: Redwood Optimize includes eval tooling that runs prompt sets against model versions and alerts on regressions. For Dedicated you can do canary rollouts with traffic split and automatic rollback based on latency/error KPIs.
[04:30] Maya: A common ask: what benchmarks do we need to validate? We usually run latency at target p95 with your median payload and peak burst simulation, cost per 1M tokens, and throughput tests across sequence length distributions.
[04:41] Elena: We'll want you to run an in-region benchmark that mirrors our 8k contexts and mixed chat/batch traffic. Can you do that as a POC?
[04:47] Ravi: Yes — typically we run a two-week POC: week one run benchmarks with representative traffic and week two implement tuning (batching, KV cache, quantization) and show improved cost/latency. We can provide the benchmark harness and collect traces.
[04:59] Tom: About network — we need VPC peering or private link for control-plane communication if Dedicated is used. Can you support that?
[05:06] Maya: We support PrivateLink and customer VPC peering for Dedicated; for Private deployment you bring the control plane into your VPC. We'll document the network ports and egress requirements.
[05:14] Priya: One more on security: can keys be kept in our KMS and never leave? For encryption at rest and in transit?
[05:20] Ravi: For the Dedicated offering we support customer-managed keys for data at rest and key wrapping; ephemeral keys for in-flight are rotated and we can document HSM usage if needed. Private gives the most control.
[05:28] Elena: Let's talk timeline — we want to be in production by end of Q1, roughly 3 months. What does onboarding look like?
[05:35] Maya: Typical onboarding: contract and SOW first, then a kickoff, one-week benchmark run, one week tuning, then a pilot for internal apps, followed by ramped rollout. For Dedicated provisioning is fastest if you already have capacity commitments; we'll prioritize your region.
[05:46] Tom: Pricing — can you send sample committed tiers and an example calculation for our expected 200 rps baseline and bursts?
[05:51] Maya: Absolutely. We'll share dedicated pricing tiers, burst rates, and some example math. We'll also include a comparison versus hosted to show unit economics.
[05:58] Priya: Do you have EDR/endpoint policies for agents? How is access managed for ops?
[06:03] Ravi: Access is via SSO with role-based permissions; ops access can be restricted. We can integrate with your identity provider and enforce SCIM. Agent hosts are hardened; we can provide our hardening checklist.
[06:13] Elena: Any competitors or other vendors you see customers using for similar patterns?
[06:16] Maya: We're seeing folks evaluate OpenAI (hosted), Anthropic, and cloud-native options like AWS Bedrock and self-hosted runtimes that manage infra. Each has different tradeoffs on control vs speed to market.
[06:27] Tom: Okay that aligns. Next — action items?
[06:30] Maya: I'll recap after the call but quick commit items: we'll run a benchmark POC, share pricing and security pack, and collect your workload metrics.
[06:38] Elena: Sounds good.
[06:40] Maya: Anything else?
[06:42] Priya: Please include an example contract clause around data residency and audit access.
[06:46] Maya: We'll include that.
[06:48] Elena: Thanks, everyone.
[06:50] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.
[06:53] [end of recording — automated note: transcription quality medium, occasional speaker attribution errors]
